newsitem.title: USA: Massachusetts Senate race for the rich.
newsitem.headline: Massachusetts Senate race for the rich.

text.p: Two brawling Boston brahmins duking it out for the Massachusetts Senate seat threatened Thursday to use their personal fortunes in one of the most closely watched races in the country.

Democratic incumbent John Kerry, who became the richest member of Congress last year when he married Teresa Heinz, heiress to the ketchup empire, has accused Republican Gov. William Weld of breaking a spending cap that the two had earlier agreed upon.
The millionaire-politicians displayed a bit of Yankee frugality earlier this year when they agreed to a $6.9 million limit on spending.
Weld, himself from an old and wealthy New England family, agreed to the $6.9 million spending limit to keep Kerry from dipping into his wife's more than $600 million fortune.

But Kerry, who has only a razor-thin lead in opinion polls over the popular Republican governor, has less money in his campaign war chest with just three weeks before the Nov. 5 election, according to federal filings.
The Kerry campaign accused Weld of planning to break the agreement by spending excessively on media advertisements.

"We are forced to conclude that you will continue to ignore the (spending) agreement and proceed with your plan to flagrantly overspend the media expenditure limit by more than $400,000," Kerry campaign treasurer William Elsbree said in a letter to the Weld campaign on Wednesday.
Weld campaign spokesman Rob Gray said Kerry was trying to "create some confusion as an excuse to try to break the cap."

"It seems to us that they are seriously considering breaking the cap," Gray told Reuters. "We believe that this is an integrity issue for Senator Kerry. We will keep our agreement to the spending cap agreement."

Massachusetts has produced such prominent Democrats as the Kennedys and former Speaker of the House of Representatives Tip O'Neil, but the two-term Republican governor has gained support by vanquishing the state's "Taxachusetts" nickname with tax cuts and balanced budgets.
The Boston Herald on Thursday endorsed Weld for the Senate, writing that his ability to cut taxes over the past six years is needed in Washington.

"Unlike Kerry, Weld doesn't look for reasons to vote against federal tax cuts," the Herald said. "Bill Weld is for a federal balanced budget amendment, unlike the incumbent who pays lip service to the concept but who has twice cast the deciding vote agaisnt such an amendment."
Kerry has laboured two terms in the shadow of the state's senior senator, Edward Kennedy.
The race, marked by few personal attacks and mud-slinging, has been a statistical dead heat through most of the year.

Weld took the lead after launching a negative TV ad campaign, but Kerry rebounded in September and, according to polls released on Thursday, his slightly combative performance in Tuesday night's debate now have given him a narrow lead.
